notes: Shared crop library ('crops', each crop defined once) plus region packs ('packs') that list which crops apply and their local timing, stage lengths and nitrogen amounts.
Every non-null value names its source id in the entry's 'sources' map. Null = not yet sourced; backend/crops.py lists them. Never fill a number without a source.
Temperate packs use calendar windows: USDA 'most active' planting/harvest spans (MM-DD). A crop's rotation year is its harvest year, so winter wheat is planted the fall before.
Tropical packs time planting relative to the rainy season found by climate_shift.py: plant_after = {event: onset|end, days: [earliest, latest]}. Harvest = planting + total stage_days.
stage_days are FAO-56 Table 11 lengths (initial, development, mid, late) from the row closest to the pack's climate; the row used is named in stage_note.
Kc ini values are FAO-56 Table 12 crop-group values (the per-crop column is an image on the FAO page). Where a source gives a range, it is kept as [low, high].

ky = FAO-33 seasonal yield response factor (> 1 drought sensitive, < 1 tolerant). drought_tolerance (1-5) stays null until a source with a ranked scale is found; ky is not converted because it measures yield loss per water shortfall, not survival.
base_temp_c and heat.threshold_c are mean daily temperatures. heat.kind says whether the threshold is where grain yield fails (USDA TB1935) or where yield starts to drop (FAO).
gdd_required uses the same 86/50 F method as climate_shift.py, in C-days (F-days x 5/9).

n_effect is the crop's class (fixes / neutral / heavy_feeder). Amounts are regional, so they live in the pack: n_need_kg_ha = fertilizer N for the crop; next_crop_n_adjust_kg_ha = change to the next crop's N rate (negative = credit) by the next crop's n_season (warm/cool, K-State MF2586). lb/acre converted at 1.121 kg/ha per lb/acre.
soil_preferences textures use the USDA class names from soil_client.texture_class.

maize.name: Maize (corn, grain)
maize.soil_note: FAO: does well on most soils but less so on very heavy dense clay and very sandy soils; susceptible to waterlogging.

soybean.name: Soybean
soybean.gdd_note: Not applicable: FAO describes soybean as a short-day plant whose flowering depends on daylength.
soybean.soil_note: FAO: wide range of soils except very sandy; sensitive to waterlogging; optimum pH 6 to 6.5.

winter_wheat.name: Wheat (winter-sown)
winter_wheat.kc_note: FAO row 'Winter wheat, with frozen soils'
winter_wheat.gdd_note: Not applicable: winter wheat needs vernalization over winter, so a base-10 C season total does not describe it.
winter_wheat.soil_note: FAO: wide range of soils but medium textures are preferred; optimum pH 6 to 8.

oats.name: Oats (spring)
oats.rooting_note: FAO-56 Table 22 has no oats row; spring wheat row used.
oats.ky_note: FAO-33 Table 1 has no oats row.

alfalfa.name: Alfalfa (hay)
alfalfa.kc_note: FAO row 'Alfalfa hay, averaged cutting effects'
alfalfa.heat_note: Hay crop: no grain-set stage, so a reproductive failure temperature does not apply.
alfalfa.soil_note: UMN: prefers well-drained, deep soils; keeping pH between 6.5 and 7.0 is extremely important.

sorghum.name: Sorghum (grain)
sorghum.soil_note: FAO: does well on most soils but better in light to medium textured soils; preferably well-aerated and well-drained.

sunflower.name: Sunflower
sunflower.soil_note: FAO: grown on a wide range of soils; under low rainfall needs a deep soil with good water holding capacity; optimum pH 6.0 to 7.5.

pigeon_pea.name: Pigeon pea
pigeon_pea.kc_note: FAO-56 Tables 11, 12 and 22 have no pigeon pea row.

groundnut.name: Groundnut (peanut)
groundnut.heat_note: FAO: optimum mean daily temperature 22 to 28 C; yield drops above 33 C and below 18 C.
groundnut.soil_note: FAO: well-drained, loose, friable medium textured soils; below pH 6 liming may be necessary.

rice.name: Rice
rice.depletion_note: FAO-56: rice p is relative to saturation, not field capacity.

cereal_rye.name: Cereal rye
cereal_rye.cover_note: min_days_before_first_frost = 0 is our reading of SARE's 'late fall is tolerated'; rye survives to spring even when planted late.
